questions.enonce_markdown:
**3.** (a) Given A, B, and C as true statements and X, Y and Z as false statements, determine the truth-values of the following compound statements:

(i) $[(A \vee B) \cdot Y] \equiv (X \cdot Y) \supset C$

(ii) $[\sim X \supset (A \vee B)] \supset (C \cdot Y)$

(iii) $(A \cdot B) \vee (X \supset Y)$

(3x3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Values: $A = B = C = T$ and $X = Y = Z = F$.

**(i) $[(A \vee B) \cdot Y] \equiv (X \cdot Y) \supset C$ (3 marks).** The main connective is $\equiv$: the left side is $[(A \vee B) \cdot Y]$ and the right side is $[(X \cdot Y) \supset C]$.

- Left side: $(T \vee T) \cdot F = T \cdot F = F$.
- Right side: $(F \cdot F) \supset T = F \supset T = T$.
- Whole: $F \equiv T = F$.

The statement is **false**.

**(ii) $[\sim X \supset (A \vee B)] \supset (C \cdot Y)$ (3 marks).**

- $\sim X = \sim F = T$ and $A \vee B = T$, so $[\sim X \supset (A \vee B)] = T \supset T = T$.
- $C \cdot Y = T \cdot F = F$.
- Whole: $T \supset F = F$.

The statement is **false**.

**(iii) $(A \cdot B) \vee (X \supset Y)$ (3 marks).**

- $A \cdot B = T \cdot T = T$ (and $X \supset Y = F \supset F = T$).
- Whole: $T \vee T = T$ (one true disjunct is enough).

The statement is **true**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Using the suggested annotations, translate the following into logical notations of propositional functions:

(i) All obedient people are law abiding citizens. Cameroonians are obedient people. Therefore, they are law-abiding citizens. (Ox: x is an obedient people; Cx: x is a law-abiding citizen; Ex: x is a Cameroonian).

(ii) Some footballers are not patient persons. All nurses are patient persons. Hence, some nurses are not footballers. (Fx : x is a footballer ; Px : x is a patient person; Nx : x is a nurse).

(iii) If a man is prayerful, he is always God fearing. Thus all devoted Christians are God fearing persons. (Mx : x is a prayerful man ; Gx : x is a God fearing persons ; Dx : x is a devoted Christian).

(3 x 3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (3 marks).**

- Premise 1 (A proposition): $(x)(Ox \supset Cx)$
- Premise 2 (A proposition): $(x)(Ex \supset Ox)$
- Conclusion: $(x)(Ex \supset Cx)$

In one line: $(x)(Ox \supset Cx),\ (x)(Ex \supset Ox)\ /\ \therefore\ (x)(Ex \supset Cx)$. (This is a valid argument of the form Barbara.)

**(ii) (3 marks).** "Some ... are not ..." is the existential negative; "All ... are ..." is the universal conditional.

- Premise 1 (O proposition): $(\exists x)(Fx \cdot \sim Px)$
- Premise 2 (A proposition): $(x)(Nx \supset Px)$
- Conclusion (O proposition): $(\exists x)(Nx \cdot \sim Fx)$

In one line: $(\exists x)(Fx \cdot \sim Px),\ (x)(Nx \supset Px)\ /\ \therefore\ (\exists x)(Nx \cdot \sim Fx)$. (Translation only is required. The argument is in fact invalid: take one footballer who is not patient and one nurse who is also a footballer and is patient; both premises are true, but no nurse fails to be a footballer, so the conclusion is false.)

**(iii) (3 marks).**

- Premise: $(x)(Mx \supset Gx)$ ("if a man is prayerful, he is always God fearing")
- Conclusion: $(x)(Dx \supset Gx)$

In one line: $(x)(Mx \supset Gx)\ /\ \therefore\ (x)(Dx \supset Gx)$. (Translation only is required. As printed, the argument is an enthymeme: the missing premise $(x)(Dx \supset Mx)$, "devoted Christians are prayerful", is needed to make it valid.)

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) Annotate the following formal proofs of validity for the following arguments by stating the justification for each

(i)

$\sim A$

$A \vee C$

$(A \supset B) \cdot (C \supset D)\ /\ \therefore\ B \vee D$

(ii)

$X \cdot Y$

$X$

$(X \cdot Y) \vee \sim Z\ /\ \therefore\ \sim Z$

(iii)

$J$

$J \supset K\ /\ \therefore\ K$

(3 x 2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) (2 marks).**

| Line | Statement | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\sim A$ | Premise |
| 2 | $A \vee C$ | Premise |
| 3 | $(A \supset B) \cdot (C \supset D)$ | Premise |
| 4 | $C$ | 1, 2, Disjunctive Syllogism (DS) |
| 5 | $B \vee D$ | 3, 2, Constructive Dilemma (CD) |

The argument is valid: $B \vee D$ follows directly from the dilemma premises (line 3) and the disjunction of the antecedents (line 2).

**(ii) (2 marks).**

| Line | Statement | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $X \cdot Y$ | Premise |
| 2 | $X$ | 1, Simplification (Simp) |
| 3 | $(X \cdot Y) \vee \sim Z$ | Premise |

No rule of inference gives the conclusion $\sim Z$ from these lines. Disjunctive Syllogism would need the denial of $X \cdot Y$, but line 1 asserts $X \cdot Y$. In fact the argument **as printed is invalid**: with $X = Y = Z = T$ the three premises are true ($X \cdot Y = T$; $X = T$; $(X \cdot Y) \vee \sim Z = T \vee F = T$) while the conclusion $\sim Z$ is false. The printed third premise is probably a misprint of a conditional: if it reads $(X \cdot Y) \supset \sim Z$, then line 4 is $\sim Z$ (1, 3, Modus Ponens (MP)) and the argument is valid.

**(iii) (2 marks).**

| Line | Statement | Justification |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $J$ | Premise |
| 2 | $J \supset K$ | Premise |
| 3 | $K$ | 1, 2, Modus Ponens (MP) |

questions.enonce_markdown: (d) Symbolise this argument: "Either the inspector comes or the seminar would not hold." (1 mark)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Let $I$ = the inspector comes; $S$ = the seminar holds ("would not hold" is the negation of $S$). "Either ... or ..." is the disjunction:

$$I \vee \sim S$$

(The statement is a single disjunctive proposition, not an argument with a conclusion.)
